title: Files, processes and streams
bridge: Node's fs, child_process and stream modules are like the File and fetch APIs in the browser. Except: they reach the real disk and real programs on the machine. A strange file name can become a command, and a big file can fill memory, unless you use execFile and streams.
intro: The harness reads its task from a file, runs git and test tools, and saves logs. The gateway passes long model answers through without holding them. This lesson teaches the three Node tools behind that: fs/promises, execFile and streams.

picture.caption: Read a task, run git safely, and move a big file through a stream in small chunks.

steps.text: readFile and JSON.parse: the task for this run
execFile("git", ["rev-parse", ...]): a list of arguments, no shell
stdout comes back as a string; a failure comes back as an error with the exit code
the file flows in chunks of 64 KB; the tap counts each one and passes it on
gzip writes the result; memory stays small whatever the file size

sections.h: Read and write files with fs/promises
p: node:fs/promises gives async functions for files: readFile, writeFile, mkdir. The harness reads /run/nova/task.json the same way and writes /run/nova/status.json.
In an ES module you can await at the top level, so a small script needs no main function. JSON.parse returns any, so we cast it here; lesson p1-5 replaces the cast with a real check.
sections.because: We use the promise versions because they read like the async code you write in React, with no callbacks.

notes.text: The node: prefix says this is built into Node, not a package from npm.
"utf8" returns a string; without it you get a Buffer of bytes. The cast is a promise to tsc, not a check.
Runs git and waits. stdout is what git printed, with a newline at the end.
Creates runs/out and any missing parents, and does not fail if it exists.
Writes the whole string at once. Fine for small files; big ones use streams (below).

sections.see: task RH-1234 at bf27ec8: Fix the empty table state
sections.ifInstead: If instead you see ENOENT: no such file or directory, open 'runs/task.json', run the script from ~/p1-lab, where runs/ is.

p: execFile starts a program with a list of arguments and collects what it prints. promisify turns its callback into a promise, so you can await it. The result has stdout and stderr.
The harness's checkpoint (G3-26) runs git this way: a small git() helper, then add, commit and push. The kb_search tool runs the kb CLI the same way.
sections.because: We wrap execFile in a small git() helper, so every git call has the same folder and the same safe form.

code.file: ai-agents/harness/src/checkpoint.ts (G3-26, shortened: the start of checkpoint())

notes.text: /work/fcp is the checkout on every VM, so each git call runs there.
git diff --quiet answers with its exit code: 0 means no changes, 1 means changes.
A non-zero exit rejects the promise. Here that rejection means 'yes, something is staged'.
step.title comes from a model. As one argument it can never become a command.

p: exec, without File, runs your string through /bin/sh. Quotes, $( ) and ; in the string are then shell syntax. A Jira title is text from a person, and a title with a quote in it can run a command.
execFile passes each argument straight to the program, with no shell in between. Whatever the text holds, it stays one argument.
sections.because: We show the attack once because 'escape the quotes' feels safe, and it is not.

notes.text: The quote closes the string in the shell, and echo INJECTED becomes a second command.
The shell sees: echo "oops"; echo INJECTED; echo "". Three commands.
echo gets one argument, the whole title, and prints it back unchanged.

callout.text: Platform code never builds a shell string from input. Ticket text, branch names, file names and model output go in an argument list.

p: If the program exits with a non-zero code, the promise rejects. The error has code (the exit code), stdout and stderr. If the program is not installed at all, the error says spawn <name> ENOENT.
Read the exit code before you treat a failure as a crash. Some tools, like git diff --quiet, use it as an answer.
sections.because: We read code and stderr because the message a person needs is in stderr, not in the stack trace.

notes.text: git exits with 128 because nope is not a commit.
For a program that ran, code is its exit code.
For a program that does not exist, code is the string ENOENT.

sections.see:
code 128 stderr fatal: ambiguous argument 'nope': unknown revision or path not in the working tree.
Error: spawn gti ENOENT

p: A stream moves data in chunks, about 64 KB at a time, instead of all at once. A readable stream gives chunks, a writable one takes them, and a Transform sits in the middle and may change them.

pipeline connects them, waits until the last chunk is written, and closes every stream if one fails. The gateway does this with a model's answer. A Transform called tap feeds each chunk to the meter and passes it on.
sections.because: We stream because a 67 MB log, or a model answer that takes minutes, should never sit whole in memory.

notes.text: A Transform is a stream you write: chunks go in, chunks come out.
Hands the same chunk to the next stream. The gateway's tap does exactly this after meter.feed(chunk).
Read, count, compress, write. The promise settles when the file is closed, or rejects on the first error.
rss is all the memory the process holds. It stays near 100 MB however big the file is.

sections.see: read 66.8 MB; memory in use 94.3 MB

p: Node 24 has fetch built in. res.body is a web stream, the kind browsers use. Readable.fromWeb turns it into a Node stream, so pipeline can write it to a file or to an HTTP response.
The gateway streams Anthropic's answer to the VM like this, chunk by chunk, so the agent sees tokens as they arrive.
sections.because: We convert the web stream once at the edge because every Node tool, pipeline included, expects a Node stream.

notes.text: Only the type, for the cast below. verbatimModuleSyntax wants import type for it.
fetch does not throw on 404 or 500; check ok yourself.
Web stream in, Node stream out. The cast fixes a known mismatch between fetch's types and node:stream/web.

sections.ifInstead: If instead tsc says 'Argument of type ReadableStream<Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>> is not assignable', add the as ReadableStream cast and the import type line.

quiz.q: A Jira title goes into git commit -m. Which call is safe?

options.text: exec(`git commit -m "${title}"`) after replacing every " with \"
options.why: The shell has many special characters: $( ), backticks, newlines. Escaping by hand misses some.
No shell runs, so the title stays one argument whatever it contains.
JSON quoting is not shell quoting; $( ) inside double quotes still runs.

quiz.q: In checkpoint.ts, git diff --cached --quiet rejects with exit code 1. What does the code conclude?

options.text: git crashed, so the checkpoint fails
options.why: For --quiet, exit 1 is an answer, not a crash.

options.text: Nothing is staged, so there is nothing to commit
Something is staged, so it commits
options.why: The then(() => false, () => true) turns the rejection into staged = true.

quiz.q: Why does the gateway pass Anthropic's answer through pipeline instead of await res.text()?

options.text: The VM sees tokens as they arrive, memory stays small, and an error closes both sides
options.why: Streaming keeps the agent responsive and the gateway light, and pipeline handles failures.

options.text: Because res.text() does not exist in Node
options.why: It exists; it waits for the whole body first.

options.text: Because pipeline makes the model answer faster
options.why: The model is as fast either way; streaming changes when you see the tokens.

words.plain: Node's async file functions: readFile, writeFile, mkdir.
Starts a program with a list of arguments and no shell; collects stdout and stderr.
When text put into a shell string runs as a command because of quotes or $( ).
The number a program ends with: 0 means success; others mean failure or an answer.
Data that moves in chunks, so a big file or a long answer never sits whole in memory.
A stream in the middle of a pipeline that sees each chunk and may change it.
Connects streams, waits for the end, and closes all of them if one fails.

tickets.why: checkpoint.ts runs git through execFile with an argument list, and reads git's exit codes.
The gateway streams the model's answer through a Transform tap with pipeline and Readable.fromWeb.
frontend/scripts/verify.ts runs git and the tools with execFileSync, never a shell string.
The BYTE-GOLD miner reads fcp's history with execFileSync and git log.

remember: Files with fs/promises, programs with execFile and an argument list, big data with streams and pipeline.
